claims.statement: The control-plane worker exposes three platform handlers in src/index.ts: a fetch handler that routes WebSocket upgrades to the SessionDO and all other requests to router.ts, a scheduled handler that dispatches on event.cron between the image-build scheduler (7,37 * * * *), the abandoned-draft sweep (23 * * * *), and the every-minute automation tick plus Autofix queue health check, and a queue handler that routes by isAutofixQueue to either the Autofix consumer or the image-build finalization consumer.

The WebSocket upgrade path matches /sessions/:id/ws, verifies the session exists via the D1 SessionIndexStore (404 when unknown), and forwards the upgrade to the Session Durable Object resolved by env.SESSION.idFromName(sessionId), adding CORS headers to the 101 response; connection authentication beyond the upgrade is re-checked inside the DO.

Queue routing in the worker's queue() handler classifies a batch by the isAutofixQueue prefix check (queues named open-inspect-github-autofix-*); all other queues go to image-build finalization. The prefix-based check is deliberate so an image-build finalization queue whose deployment name merely contains 'github-autofix' is not misrouted.

handleRequest in router.ts runs the full request pipeline: it rejects a missing env.DB once with 503 as the single honest boundary (so ctx.db is always present in handlers), builds the RequestContext with trace/request IDs and per-request metrics, answers CORS preflights before matching, matches routes by method and compiled regex, authenticates non-public routes, enforces the SCM provider gate, executes the handler with HttpError mapped centrally and other errors logged as generic 500, and wraps every response with CORS, x-request-id, x-trace-id, optional route cacheControl, and the http.request wide event.

Every control-plane response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, x-request-id (an 8-character UUID), and x-trace-id (from the inbound x-trace-id header or a fresh UUID); these correlation IDs propagate through logs and are forwarded on internal DO fetches by the session runtime client.

src/routes/shared.ts provides the shared route framework: defineRoute/defineRoutes attach a RoutePolicy (authentication kind plus supportedScmProviders) to a route definition and narrow the handler's principal type; parsePattern converts :name segments into named regex groups; json/error/HttpError give uniform responses with HttpError mapped centrally by the router's dispatch catch.

RouteAuthentication variants are public, handler-authenticated, web-service, user, user-or-service, sandbox (path-bound via getSessionId), and user-or-service-with-sandbox-fallback; named policy constants pin the standard combinations (GITHUB_USER_OR_SERVICE_ROUTE, SCM_AGNOSTIC_* variants, SCM_CREDENTIALS_ROUTE, sandbox-fallback variants).

enforceImplementedScmProvider returns an explicit 501 with a per-deployment message when a route's supportedScmProviders excludes the deployment's SCM_PROVIDER (e.g. bitbucket), and 500 when the SCM_PROVIDER value itself is invalid; the deployment SCM provider resolution is memoized per isolate keyed on the env value.

The router's route table composes the full API surface from per-domain route modules: browser-auth, sign-in-providers, sessions (create, index, runtime proxy, ws-token, prompt, PRs, media, attachments, diffs, skills, child spawn/children), slack-notify, repos, secrets, environments and environment-secrets, image-builds, model-preferences, model-provider-accounts, integration-settings, commit-signing, scm-settings, automations, mcp-servers, analytics, autofix, skills, keyboard-shortcuts, and webhooks (sentry, automation, github, slack); GET /health is the only public route.

A policy-table test (router.policy.test.ts) pins the authentication kind of representative routes from each family (public health, handler-authenticated webhooks and image-build callbacks, web-service auth routes, human-user-restricted routes, sandbox routes with the bound session id, and sandbox-fallback session routes), so accidental policy changes fail fast.

Every non-public, non-sandbox request resolves to exactly one typed Principal before its handler runs — user (canonical userId), service (service name plus optionally asserted actor), or sandbox (sessionId); enforceRoutePrincipal additionally rejects non-web services on web-service routes with 401 and non-user principals on user routes with 403.

User authentication composes two credentials: a sig1 service signature over the service:web channel verified first, then — only when the route requires webService: user — a Better Auth opaque session cookie validated by a non-refreshing session read so resource requests never extend expiry; the resulting user principal carries the canonical users.id plus provider-independent browser-session evidence, and a malformed or cross-user session raises SessionIntegrityError mapped to 500.

The Better Auth runtime is built from a normalized config (BROWSER_AUTH_SECRET of at least 32 chars, exact HTTPS WEB_APP_URL origin with HTTP loopback allowed locally, complete GitHub/Google OAuth credential pairs where partial pairs throw, and at least one enabled provider) and is memoized per env.DB object with a configuration fingerprint — which is why the router's composition root passes the raw binding, not the per-request instrumented wrapper, as the cache key.

Sign-in admission is gated by the AdmissionPolicy: allowlists of GitHub usernames, emails, email domains, and GitHub organizations (membership checked via the GitHub API, with API unavailability failing closed as AdmissionUnavailableError), or UNSAFE_ALLOW_ALL_USERS; each configured provider must be expressible under the configured allowlists or construction throws — Google requires provider-neutral email/domain rules.

Worker-to-worker service traffic signs requests with the per-service sig1 HMAC format binding method, path, canonicalized query, body SHA-256, asserted actor, timestamp, and nonce; the control plane holds one verification key per service (SERVICE_AUTH_SECRET_* — an absent key is a 500 misconfiguration), freshness-checks the header before buffering the body, caps bodies at 16 MiB, performs log-only nonce-reuse detection, enforces per-service actor-namespace assertion rights, and rebuilds the consumed body before the handler sees the request.

Sandbox routes authenticate with a Bearer token verified by a round-trip to the owning session Durable Object (/internal/verify-sandbox-token), which on success sets the sandbox principal; a failed verification is 401, an unreachable DO is 503, and on user-or-service-with-sandbox-fallback routes the sandbox token is tried only when the sig1 attempt failed with failedScheme none — a recognized-but-failed service credential is terminal, so a bot signature can never be exchanged for sandbox access.

POST /sessions/:id/ws-token derives the participant identity from the verified principal (rejecting caller-supplied identity and SCM token body fields), forwards to the DO's /internal/ws-token where the WsTokenHandler upserts the participant (coalescing client-sent SCM tokens against newer server-side refreshes) and rotates a 32-byte WebSocket token stored only as a hash; at subscribe time the DO re-hashes the presented token and enforces a 24-hour TTL, closing stale sockets with code 4001.

Handler-authenticated webhook routes verify their own credentials: automation webhooks require a Bearer API key verified as a timing-safe SHA-256 hash (32-byte base64url key, rotatable via POST /automations/:id/regenerate-key) with a 64 KB payload cap; Sentry webhooks verify the sentry-hook-signature HMAC against the automation's AES-256-GCM-encrypted client secret with a 256 KB cap; image-build callbacks authenticate with single-use bearer tokens hashed under the dedicated IMAGE_CALLBACK_TOKEN_PEPPER and bound to the exact provider session id.

Internal normalized event endpoints (/internal/github-event, /internal/slack-event) accept only the matching bot's service principal per requireEventPoster, validate the normalized event envelope, and forward to the scheduler; the GitHub path additionally tracks PR lifecycle state in a BackgroundTasks submission whose failure never affects automation matching.

Identity enforcement (applyIdentityEnforcement) closes the auth-to-authorization loop for identity-minting routes: participant identity is derived from the verified principal, forbidden body identity/SCM fields are rejected with 400, and session-create, ws-token, and automation-create fail closed with 403 when no user identity can be derived.

The SqlDatabase port in db/sql-database.ts is the engine-neutral surface all stores use (prepare and batch); D1Database satisfies it structurally via a compile-time assertion so no runtime wrapper exists. The contract types cannot express: batch executes atomically in order with positionally 1:1 results, and meta.changes must carry real affected-row counts because ~38 call sites gate correctness (CAS conflicts, guarded transitions) on it. It is distinct from the session DO's synchronous SqlStorage, which is intentionally not covered.

The D1 layer keeps one store file per aggregate (session-index, automation-store, image-builds, environments, repo-metadata, repo-secrets, global-secrets, user-store, mcp-servers, skills, model-provider-accounts, etc.), each taking the SqlDatabase port in its constructor and mapping snake_case database rows to camelCase API types.

instrumentD1 wraps the SqlDatabase port so every query records wall-clock time plus engine metadata (server duration, rows read/written) into the per-request RequestMetrics; batch unwraps instrumented statements via the ORIGINAL_STMT symbol before delegating, and summarize() flattens the collector into d1_query_count, d1_total_ms, d1_server_total_ms, d1_rows_read/d1_rows_written plus named spans, spread into the http.request wide event. Stores receive the instrumented handle transparently with no store changes.

env.DB is read exactly once per composition root — the router's request path, the SessionDO constructor, and the scheduled/queue handlers in index.ts — with every other consumer taking the injected SqlDatabase (ctx.db, this.db, or a constructor parameter); an ESLint no-restricted-syntax rule bans .DB member reads in control-plane source, and each composition root carries an inline eslint-disable with justification. In SessionDO, this.db (D1) is deliberately distinct from this.sql (DO-embedded SQLite).

BackgroundTasks (platform-ports.ts) is the ctx.waitUntil seam for deferring work past the current request; the Cloudflare adapter invokes the task factory synchronously inside submit, absorbs a synchronous factory throw exactly like a later rejection (building a task can never fail the caller), and logs failures as background_task.failed. A contract-faithful test double mirrors the production boundary so collaborator tests exercise the same contract.

BackgroundTasks callers include the PR-lifecycle tracker on GitHub webhooks (best-effort, additive to automation matching) and the image-build save hooks, which submit a detached best-effort trigger so a build-trigger failure never fails the CRUD operation that invoked it.

The worker's scheduled handler recognizes exactly three crons — the every-minute automation tick (* * * * *), the image-build scheduler (7,37 * * * *), and the abandoned-draft sweep (23 * * * *) — logging unknown triggers and doing nothing; Terraform registers exactly these three schedules and its configuration comment requires them to match the code constants IMAGE_BUILD_SCHEDULER_CRON and ABANDONED_DRAFT_SWEEP_CRON.

The Scheduler is the request-driven automation engine invoked by the tick, automation routes, and SessionDO completion callbacks. Each tick first runs the recovery sweep, then processes up to MAX_PER_TICK (25) overdue automations through startInvocation, bounded by a per-tick child-launch budget of 50 subrequest-costly launches (whole automations deferred to the next tick when the budget would overflow) and a launch concurrency of 4 to smooth sandbox cold starts.

The tick's recovery sweep bulk-fails orphaned starting runs (no session claimed within 5 minutes) and timed-out running runs (EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_MS, default 90 minutes), then applies per-invocation failure accounting; a finalization sweep re-applies missed failure strikes and streak resets for invocations in the last 24 hours — covering the crash window between a child's terminal update and its callback — through the same CAS-guarded, idempotent helper as live callbacks.

startInvocation is the single firing pipeline behind tick, manual trigger, and events: overlap scoping is automation-wide for schedule/manual firings but per concurrency_key for events (so PR #42 and #43 don't serialize); the guarded atomic batch insert of invocation plus children includes the schedule advance; a UNIQUE collision (cron double-fire, event replay) re-advances the schedule monotonically and stands down as deduplicated; manual overlap records nothing and surfaces as AutomationTriggerBlockedError mapped to 409. Each firing records one invocation that fans out into one child run per target (repository or environment; no targets means one repo-less child), with failing repository resolution pre-failing its child without blocking siblings and provider auth/targets snapshotted before admission so later edits never rewrite in-flight history.

An automation invocation's status is derived, never stored: DERIVED_INVOCATION_STATUS_SQL in automation-store.ts is the single SQL definition (with a TS twin the integration tests keep in lockstep) mapping child-run aggregates to skipped, starting, running, completed, failed, or partial_failed.

The automation consecutive-failure counter is incremented at most once per invocation — the failure_counted_at compare-and-set admits a single winner across concurrent callbacks, launch failures, and sweeps — and three consecutive failures auto-pause the automation (scheduler.auto_pause); a fully-completed invocation resets the streak. Pre-failed and launch-failed children apply the strike immediately, which is also the born-terminal path that finalizes an invocation whose every child failed.

The Scheduler.runComplete callback from SessionDO transitions only an active run to terminal via a SQL guard, so a late callback after recovery-sweep failure or a racing duplicate is acknowledged as ignored — a terminal child never transitions twice; Slack-triggered runs additionally post completion to the triggering thread through the SLACK_BOT service binding, signed with the destination bot's own per-service secret (callback-signing.ts).

runImageBuildScheduler (twice hourly) assembles the provider-neutral ImageBuildScheduler and runs each phase independently so one failure cannot skip the rest: republish recoverable finalizations to the Queue, mark stale building rows failed after the maximum provider-session lifetime plus dispatch grace, cleanup terminal builds' provider sessions at bounded concurrency, reconcile scopes (only when an image provider from SANDBOX_PROVIDER among modal/vercel/opencomputer/e2b and a source-control provider are configured, evaluating the rebuild policy and confirming branch drift with head lookups before triggerBuildWithTarget), and reap failed/superseded artifacts best-effort with a stats line logged per tick.

Stale-build detection is sized at the longest provider-session lifetime (build timeout plus the 10-minute finalization grace) plus a 5-minute dispatch grace, measured from row registration, so a long-but-live build is never reaped; the blast radius of misclassification is only a redundant rebuild because the status = 'building' completion guards reject a misclassified build's late callback.

The abandoned-draft sweep (hourly at :23, deliberately offset from the image-build cron and on its own cron because retention is measured in hours) retires warm sessions that were never prompted: it lists up to 50 candidates oldest-first from the D1 index and asks each session DO (/internal/expire-draft, 10-second timeout) to re-check the invariant and transition, reporting archived, not_draft (stale index repaired), has_work (a prompt that never dispatched), or missing (404; index row retired); the 8-hour TTL outlasts a long pause at the keyboard because a stopped sandbox respawns on the next prompt while an archived session would reject it, and errors are counted rather than thrown so a stalled session cannot hold the sweep.

All image-build trigger sources converge on ImageBuildWorkflow.triggerBuild / triggerBuildWithTarget / triggerBuildIfStale (cron, save hooks, manual routes), which enforces the per-scope concurrency-1 rule in one place; saving a scope's owning entity kicks a detached best-effort build, while changing its secrets synchronously invalidates live images before the response so rotated values can't keep serving from a stale image.

Every image-build callback authenticates with the single-use bearer token minted at trigger time — only its HMAC hash (under IMAGE_CALLBACK_TOKEN_PEPPER) is stored, bound to the exact provider session id — and the completion or failure is accepted atomically in D1 (a build not accepting the transition yields a 409 mapped error) before publishing a secret-free, versioned Queue command ({version: 1, buildId, completionHash}); the completion hash canonicalizes the accepted payload so the Queue never carries tokens or credentials and stale replays are rejected.

consumeImageBuildFinalizationBatch applies Queue delivery semantics per message — schema-invalid commands are acked (discarded), processed work is acked, and busy or failed work is retried with a delay without aborting later messages in the batch; Terraform configures the consumer with batch size 1, max concurrency 5, max retries 12, retry delay 15 s, and a dead-letter queue.

The ImageBuildFinalizer is idempotent under at-least-once delivery: a completion-hash mismatch is dropped as stale; a 6-minute lease (longer than the 5-minute provider deadline) serializes overlapping attempts, with an expired attempt that recorded no artifact failing the build rather than creating twice; the provider snapshot/checkpoint runs under a 5-minute abort deadline; artifact persistence is fenced — an ambiguous D1 failure is re-read before compensating, and an unfenced artifact is deleted or quarantined on the row if deletion also fails — then tryMarkImageBuildReady supersedes prior images for the scope and terminal cleanup removes the bound provider session idempotently.

The control-plane worker is the registered consumer of the GitHub Autofix queue (production remains owned by the github-bot): handleAutofixQueue builds the AutofixService and an AutofixQueueConsumer per batch with MAX_DELIVERY_ATTEMPTS = 5, where a permanent provider error marks the feedback failed and acks, a transient error records and retries (marking failed once attempts are exhausted), and even a schema-invalid envelope retries rather than acking.

On every automation tick the worker submits checkAutofixQueueHealth via waitUntil, inspecting the AUTOFIX_QUEUE and AUTOFIX_DLQ bindings — used read-only for metrics — and logging autofix.queue_health errors when the DLQ holds any message, the primary backlog exceeds 25, or the oldest primary message exceeds 5 minutes.

src/types.ts Env declares the shell's bindings: the SESSION Durable Object namespace, the DB D1 database, the REPOS_CACHE KV namespace (short-lived /repos listing cache), the MEDIA_BUCKET R2 bucket, the IMAGE_BUILD_FINALIZATION_QUEUE plus read-only AUTOFIX_QUEUE/AUTOFIX_DLQ bindings, optional SLACK_BOT/LINEAR_BOT service bindings, the four per-service sig1 verification secrets, the credential-encryption secret domains, and provider/deployment variables.

Production bindings are Terraform-managed: the cloudflare-worker module wires the KV/D1/R2/queue/service/DO bindings, plain-text vars, and secrets, and registers the three cron triggers and queue consumers, while generating the per-service sig1 secrets and the image-callback pepper in Terraform state; wrangler.jsonc is test-only with placeholder IDs for the Miniflare integration suite.

src/env-validation.ts enforces the encryption-key contract eagerly: requireRepoSecretsEncryptionKey and requireTokenEncryptionKey require strict base64 decoding to exactly 32 bytes of AES-256 material, failing loudly at first touch instead of running degraded — a malformed key would otherwise throw at the first secret write mid-spawn, and a short key would silently downgrade to AES-128/192.

The REPOS_CACHE KV namespace backs the /repos listing cache (5-minute fresh window, 1-hour KV TTL, stale-while-revalidate, invalidated on metadata changes) and doubles as the SCM provider cache store; MEDIA_BUCKET is the R2 bucket behind the ObjectStorage port used for media artifacts and session attachments.

The worker entrypoint exports the SessionDO Durable Object class for Cloudflare discovery and forwards its fetch, webSocketMessage, webSocketClose, webSocketError, and alarm callbacks to a per-activation session runtime built eagerly by createSessionRuntime (session/components.ts); all application wiring lives in that composition root rather than the DO class itself.

Stores and services take the SqlDatabase port as a constructor input (AutomationStore and SessionIndexStore follow the same pattern), so the same domain code runs against the raw D1 binding, the instrumented per-request handle, or a test double without modification.

The Scheduler exposes four entrypoints beyond its constructor — tick (cron), event (webhook and bot-forwarded normalized events), trigger (manual, 409 on active run), and runComplete (SessionDO completion callback) — and each constructs its own AutomationStore from the injected database.

Session routes obtain DO access through the SessionRouteContext sessionRuntime client, which resolves stubs by idFromName and stamps x-trace-id and x-request-id onto every internal request; internal paths and schemas are shared via session/contracts.ts (SessionInternalPaths) so router and SessionDO cannot drift.

The shared route module also provides the handler helpers parseJsonBody (typed JSON parsing returning an error Response on invalid bodies), extractRepoParams (validated owner/name decoding from named groups), and resolveRepoOrError (SCM provider resolution mapping 404 for uninstalled repos and permanent configuration errors surfaced as their original message).
